# Inter-process communication (IPC)

Once sim, control, and logging live in **different processes** (or machines), you need a way to move observations and commands without sharing one Python interpreter. That is **inter-process communication (IPC)** — the plumbing behind “policy process ↔ sim process,” hardware drivers, and multi-rate loops.

This chapter is conceptual: we do not ship IPC examples in `scripts/` yet. It compares three patterns you will see in robotics labs: **shared memory**, **ZeroMQ**, and **LCM**.

## Why split processes at all?

| Reason | Example |
|---|---|
| **Isolation** | Sim crash does not take down the training controller |
| **Rates** | Physics at 1 kHz, policy at 50 Hz, logger at 10 Hz |
| **Languages / stacks** | MuJoCo in C++/Python, policy in PyTorch, UI in another tool |
| **Hardware** | Motor driver daemon on the robot PC, planner on a workstation |

In-process calls (`import`, function calls) are simplest — use them until you hit one of the rows above. IPC adds **serialization, timing, and failure modes**; pick the lightest option that meets your latency and topology.

## Shared memory

**Idea:** Two processes map the **same RAM**. One writes a `numpy` buffer; the other reads it — no copy through the kernel for each frame (after setup).

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Lowest latency on **one machine** | No built-in schema — you define layout and versioning |
| High throughput for large arrays (images, state vectors) | **Synchronization is on you** (locks, semaphores, double buffering, seqlocks) |
| Simple when both sides are Python/C++ you control | Does not cross hosts; fragile if writers/readers disagree on shape/dtype |

**Python:** [`multiprocessing.shared_memory`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/multiprocessing.shared_memory.html) (3.8+), or `numpy` views into a named segment. Often paired with a small **signaling** mechanism (event, atomic counter, or a 1-byte “frame ready” flag) so the reader never sees a half-updated tensor.

**When to use:** Same workstation, **tight loop** (sim ↔ policy at hundreds–thousands of Hz), large payloads (camera + proprioception), both sides under your control. Common in embedded RL and custom sim bridges.

## ZeroMQ (ZMQ)

**Idea:** **Message sockets** — send opaque byte blobs (or structured payloads you encode) over `inproc://`, `ipc://`, or `tcp://`. Brokerless; each socket has a pattern (PUSH/PULL, PUB/SUB, REQ/REP, …).

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| **Flexible topology** — same API for threads, local processes, remote hosts | No enforced message **types** — you pick JSON, msgpack, protobuf, pickle |
| Fire-and-forget pub/sub fits telemetry and commands | Pub/sub can drop slow subscribers unless you design queues |
| Mature libraries ([PyZMQ](https://pyzmq.readthedocs.io/)) | “Which socket pattern?” is a design choice — wrong pattern → deadlocks or lost msgs |
| Good default when you might **scale out** later | Slightly higher overhead than shared memory on localhost |

**When to use:** Multiple processes **or machines**, moderate rates, you want **general-purpose** plumbing (command channel + log stream + heartbeat). Popular when the team already knows TCP and does not want multicast/LCM tooling.

## LCM (Lightweight Communications and Marshalling)

**Idea:** Robotics-oriented **typed messages** (`.lcm` definitions → generated encode/decode) over **UDP multicast** on a LAN. Strong culture of **log files** you can replay (`lcm-logger` / `lcm-logplayer`).

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| **Schema-first** messages — less “random dict over the wire” | Multicast UDP: LAN-focused; WAN/VPN needs extra care |
| Designed for **robot state + command** streams in labs | Smaller ecosystem than ZMQ outside robotics |
| Built-in **log/replay** for debugging “what did the robot see?” | Another code-gen step (`.lcm` → language bindings) |
| Low overhead for small, fixed structs at high rate | Less ideal for huge images unless you split metadata (SHM) + LCM (metadata) |

Docs: [lcm-proj.github.io](https://lcm-proj.github.io/lcm/). Common in legged robotics, MIT-style stacks, and hardware teams that standardize on a message catalog.

**When to use:** Whole lab on one subnet, many publishers/subscribers, you want **named typed messages** and **timestamped logs** — especially hardware + sim + viz on the same clock domain.

## Comparison at a glance

| | Shared memory | ZeroMQ | LCM |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Typical scope** | One machine | One machine or network | LAN (multicast) |
| **Latency (local)** | Lowest | Low–medium | Low (small messages) |
| **Message typing** | DIY layout | DIY encoding | `.lcm` schemas |
| **Best payload** | Large arrays, images | Flexible blobs / JSON | Fixed structs, state snapshots |
| **Discovery** | Shared name / fd | Connect/bind addresses | Multicast URL + channel name |
| **Replay / debug** | DIY logging | DIY logging | First-class log/replay |
| **Cross-language** | Yes (careful layout) | Yes (bytes on wire) | Yes (generated bindings) |

## Hybrid patterns (common in practice)

Nobody forces a single choice:

- **SHM for images + LCM for metadata** (width, height, timestamp, frame id).
- **ZMQ REQ/REP for commands + SHM for observations** when policy and sim are co-located but isolated.
- **LCM for robot state** + **ZMQ to a cloud trainer** — different layers of the stack.

## Choosing (rule of thumb)

1. **Same box, kHz loop, big tensors** → start with **shared memory** + explicit sync.
2. **Several services, maybe remote, general messaging** → **ZeroMQ** (pick one pattern per channel; document payloads).
3. **Lab robot bus, typed messages, multicast + logs** → **LCM** (or something LCM-shaped in your org).

Whichever you pick: define **one canonical state message** (joint `q`, `qdot`, timestamp, frame id), version it, and log enough to reproduce a bug without guessing wire format.
